question: Which category of immunodeficiency results from external factors rather than inherited mutations?
cited_learning_objective: Compare & contrast the etiology and typical presentation for major primary and secondary immunodeficiencies

options.rationale: Primary combined disorders result from mutations affecting cellular and humoral immunity. This would be correct if an inherited defect impaired both B and T cell function.
Secondary immunodeficiency develops from external factors such as infection, treatment, malnutrition, trauma, or biochemical disorders rather than an inherited mutation.
Primary antibody disorders arise from genetic defects affecting B cells or antibody production. This would be correct if the condition were inherited and predominantly impaired humoral immunity.
Primary cellular disorders arise from inherited defects affecting T cell development or function. This would be correct if a genetic abnormality caused deficient cellular immunity.
Primary innate disorders result from inherited defects involving phagocytes, complement, or related functions. This would be correct if a mutation impaired an innate immune component.

question: Which test most specifically identifies missing leukocyte populations in peripheral blood?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the principles of flow cytometry, and interpret flow cytometric dot plots to identify specific leukocyte populations (review common WBC markers learned in Block 1)

options.rationale: Serum immunoglobulin measurement quantifies antibody isotypes but does not directly enumerate specific leukocyte populations. It would be correct if the task were assessing antibody concentration.
A differential broadly counts leukocyte categories but is less specific for defined lymphocyte subsets. It would be correct if only a general distribution of white cells were required.
Complement hemolytic activity evaluates classical pathway function rather than leukocyte populations. It would be correct if recurrent infections suggested a complement defect.
Flow cytometry uses cellular markers to identify and quantify specific leukocyte populations, making it more differentiating than a routine differential.
Genotyping identifies mutations but does not directly demonstrate which circulating cell population is absent. It would be correct if a suspected molecular defect required confirmation.

question: Which immunodeficiency is caused by failure of B cell maturation beyond the pre-B cell stage?
cited_learning_objective: Compare & contrast the etiology and typical presentation for major primary and secondary immunodeficiencies

options.rationale: A BTK mutation disrupts BCR signaling, preventing maturation beyond the pre-B cell stage and markedly reducing mature B cells and all antibody classes.
Hyper-IgM syndrome has normal B cell numbers but defective class switching from impaired CD40 signaling. It would fit if IgM were increased while other isotypes were deficient.
Selective IgA deficiency preserves normal B cell numbers and other antibody isotypes. It would fit an individual older than four years with isolated low IgA.
Type II bare lymphocyte syndrome results from deficient MHC II expression and primarily reduces CD4 T cells. It would fit combined infections with low CD4 cells and low IgG.

SCID can arise from several defects affecting T cells with associated humoral dysfunction, but pre-B stage arrest specifically identifies BTK deficiency. It would fit profound early combined immune failure.

question: Which complement deficiencies are characteristically associated with recurrent Neisseria infections?
cited_learning_objective: Utilizing the patient presentation and common diagnostic test results, determine and differentiate between the various primary immunodeficiencies given a clinical case

options.rationale: Early classical pathway deficiencies are associated with bacterial infections and systemic lupus erythematosus. They would fit childhood infections accompanied by lupus manifestations.
Common gamma-chain deficiency causes X-linked SCID rather than an isolated complement susceptibility. It would fit a male infant with absent T cells and low antibodies.
C3 deficiency causes early recurrent bacterial infections, especially gram-negative sinopulmonary or invasive infections. It would fit broad bacterial susceptibility beginning shortly after birth.
NADPH oxidase deficiency causes defective phagocyte respiratory burst and susceptibility to catalase-positive bacteria and fungi. It would fit recurrent infections with granuloma formation.

options.text: C6, C7, C8, or C9 deficiency
options.rationale: Deficiency of C6 through C9 disrupts the late complement pathway and is associated with recurrent meningococcal and gonococcal infections.

question: An immune disorder produces low T cell numbers, preserved B cell numbers, and reduced antibody levels. Which defect best explains this combination?
cited_learning_objective: Utilizing the patient presentation and common diagnostic test results, determine and differentiate between the various primary immunodeficiencies given a clinical case

options.rationale: A common gamma-chain defect produces this cellular pattern, but it is specifically X-linked and is not the best general mechanism when inheritance is unspecified. It would be correct with an affected male and an X-linked pattern.
JAK3 deficiency can produce absent T cells, preserved B cells, and low antibodies. It would be correct if an autosomal recessive cytokine-signaling mutation were demonstrated.
B cells may remain numerically present while antibody production falls because deficient T cell function removes the help needed for effective humoral responses.
BTK deficiency prevents mature B cell development while preserving normal T cells. It would fit markedly reduced B cells and all antibody classes.
Selective IgA deficiency preserves both B and T cell numbers and affects only IgA. It would fit isolated low IgA with normal levels of other isotypes.

question: A disorder manifests before 6 months with bacterial, fungal, viral, and opportunistic infections. Which immune defect is most strongly suggested?
cited_learning_objective: Utilizing the patient presentation and common diagnostic test results, determine and differentiate between the various primary immunodeficiencies given a clinical case

options.rationale: Antibody deficiencies generally present after six months and predominantly cause bacterial infections. This would fit later onset with a humoral infection pattern.
Early classical pathway defects cause recurrent bacterial infections and may accompany systemic lupus erythematosus. This would fit bacterial susceptibility with low CH50.
Late complement defects characteristically produce recurrent Neisseria infections rather than broad opportunistic disease. This would fit meningococcal or gonococcal recurrence.
Very early presentation with bacterial, fungal, viral, and opportunistic infections indicates severe impairment of T cells with associated humoral dysfunction.
Selective IgA deficiency is often asymptomatic and cannot be diagnosed before age four years. It would fit later recurrent respiratory, sinus, or gastrointestinal infections with isolated low IgA.

question: Flow cytometry shows reduced CD4 cells, normal CD8 cells, and normal B cell numbers. Serum testing shows low IgG. Which diagnosis best matches these results?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the principles of flow cytometry, and interpret flow cytometric dot plots to identify specific leukocyte populations (review common WBC markers learned in Block 1)

options.rationale: MHC II deficiency reduces CD4 T cells while preserving CD8 and B cell numbers; impaired T cell help contributes to low IgG.
MHC I deficiency reduces CD8 cells while preserving CD4 cells and antibody levels. It would fit low CD8 cells with normal CD4 cells and normal immunoglobulins.
BTK deficiency markedly reduces mature B cells and all antibody classes while preserving T cells. It would fit absent B cells rather than isolated CD4 reduction.
Hyper-IgM syndrome preserves B and T cell numbers but produces increased IgM and deficient other isotypes. It would fit normal lymphocyte subsets with failed class switching.
Selective IgA deficiency preserves lymphocyte populations and IgG. It would fit isolated IgA reduction in a patient older than four years.

question: Which paired finding most strongly distinguishes MHC I deficiency from MHC II deficiency?
cited_learning_objective: Compare & contrast the etiology and typical presentation for major primary and secondary immunodeficiencies

options.rationale: Reduced CD4 cells with low IgG characterizes MHC II deficiency. It would be correct if the question asked for the pattern of type II bare lymphocyte syndrome.
Reduced B cells and broadly low antibodies characterize BTK-related agammaglobulinemia. It would fit a male child with bacterial infections beginning after six months.
Absent T cells with low antibodies is characteristic of SCID patterns rather than isolated MHC I deficiency. It would fit severe multisystem infections shortly after birth.
Normal lymphocyte populations with isolated low IgA characterize selective IgA deficiency. It would fit recurrent mucosal infections after age four years.
MHC I deficiency reduces CD8 T cells while preserving CD4 cells, B cells, and antibody levels, unlike MHC II deficiency.

question: A mutation prevents CD40 signaling in B cells despite normal B and T cell counts. Which antibody pattern should result?
cited_learning_objective: Compare & contrast the etiology and typical presentation for major primary and secondary immunodeficiencies

options.text: Decreased IgM with normal other isotypes
options.rationale: The defect does not selectively decrease IgM because B cells can still produce this initial isotype. This would require a different isolated antibody abnormality not described in the source.

options.text: Increased IgM with absent other isotypes
options.rationale: Loss of CD40 signaling prevents class switching and affinity maturation, producing increased IgM with deficiency of the other antibody isotypes.

options.text: Decreased IgA with normal other isotypes
options.rationale: This pattern characterizes selective IgA deficiency rather than failed CD40 signaling. It would fit an individual older than four years with isolated low IgA.

options.text: Decreased levels of all antibody isotypes
options.rationale: Broad depression of all antibody classes occurs when mature B cells are absent, as in BTK deficiency. It would fit reduced B cell numbers and absent germinal centers.

options.text: Normal levels of all antibody isotypes
options.rationale: Normal isotypes would indicate preserved class switching, which contradicts absent CD40 signaling. This would fit intact B cell maturation and T cell help.

question: A neutrophil assay uses a nonfluorescent substrate that becomes green after a normal respiratory burst. Which result supports NADPH oxidase deficiency?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the principles of flow cytometry, and interpret flow cytometric dot plots to identify specific leukocyte populations (review common WBC markers learned in Block 1)

options.rationale: Increased fluorescence indicates conversion of the substrate by functioning NADPH oxidase. It would support a preserved rather than deficient respiratory burst.
A normal fluorescence shift demonstrates intact oxidase-dependent substrate conversion. It would be expected in a healthy control.
Failure of dihydrorhodamine 123 to become fluorescent demonstrates a deficient respiratory burst and supports chronic granulomatous disease.
The assay described evaluates conversion to green fluorescence, not loss of a red signal. This would require a differently designed fluorescent assay.
The diagnostic test assesses neutrophil respiratory burst rather than platelet fluorescence. Platelet abnormalities would redirect evaluation toward another cellular process.

question: A child has recurrent bacterial infections, normal antibody levels, and elevated circulating neutrophils, but infected tissues contain few neutrophils. Which process is impaired?
cited_learning_objective: Utilizing the patient presentation and common diagnostic test results, determine and differentiate between the various primary immunodeficiencies given a clinical case

options.rationale: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency impairs adhesion and extravasation, leaving neutrophils in circulation while preventing their accumulation at infected sites.

Defective reactive oxygen production causes chronic granulomatous disease, in which neutrophils reach tissues but cannot kill efficiently. It would fit abnormal respiratory-burst testing and granulomas.
Defective granule trafficking causes Chédiak-Higashi syndrome. It would fit giant cytoplasmic granules, partial albinism, and progressive neurologic findings.

options.text: B cell maturation within bone marrow
options.rationale: Failure of B cell maturation causes agammaglobulinemia with reduced antibodies. It would fit absent mature B cells rather than normal antibody levels.
Complement deficiency can cause bacterial infections but does not explain failure of neutrophils to enter infected tissue. It would fit a low CH50 with otherwise normal cellular trafficking.

question: Which combination most directly links the molecular defect and diagnostic blood-smear finding in Chédiak-Higashi syndrome?
cited_learning_objective: Compare & contrast the etiology and typical presentation for major primary and secondary immunodeficiencies

options.text: BTK mutation with absent germinal centers
options.rationale: BTK mutation causes arrested B cell maturation and absent germinal centers. It would fit agammaglobulinemia rather than giant leukocyte granules.

options.text: CD40L mutation with increased serum IgM
options.rationale: CD40L mutation prevents class switching and increases IgM. It would fit hyper-IgM syndrome rather than a lysosomal trafficking disorder.

options.text: CYBB-pathway defect with absent oxidative burst
options.rationale: A defect involving NADPH oxidase produces absent respiratory burst in chronic granulomatous disease. It would fit abnormal dihydrorhodamine testing rather than enlarged granules.

options.text: LYST mutation with giant cytoplasmic granules
options.rationale: A LYST mutation disrupts lysosomal and granule trafficking, producing characteristically very large granules within leukocytes and platelets.

options.text: CD18 deficiency with absent tissue neutrophils
options.rationale: CD18 deficiency impairs leukocyte adhesion and tissue entry. It would fit absent pus, poor healing, and delayed umbilical separation.

question: A low CH50 is detected during evaluation of recurrent bacterial infections. Which follow-up test is most appropriate for localizing the defect?
cited_learning_objective: Utilizing the patient presentation and common diagnostic test results, determine and differentiate between the various primary immunodeficiencies given a clinical case

options.rationale: Antibody testing assesses humoral immunity but does not localize an abnormal classical complement pathway result. It would be appropriate if an antibody deficiency were suspected.
Lymphocyte subset analysis identifies cellular deficiencies but not the missing complement protein. It would fit suspected B or T cell deficiency.
Because normal CH50 requires all classical pathway components, a low result should be followed by measurement of individual components to identify the deficient protein.
Respiratory-burst testing evaluates NADPH oxidase function rather than complement activity. It would fit recurrent catalase-positive bacterial or fungal infections.
Adhesion-molecule genotyping evaluates leukocyte adhesion deficiency and would not localize a low CH50. It would fit delayed cord separation and absent pus.

question: Which external condition causes prolonged susceptibility by destroying memory lymphocytes and producing substantial antibody loss?
cited_learning_objective: List secondary causes of immunocompromised states

options.rationale: Chronic malaria can produce immune exhaustion affecting humoral and cellular responses. It would be correct if the mechanism emphasized exhaustion rather than memory-cell destruction.
Large burns compromise epithelial barriers and can provoke massive cytokine release. They would fit extensive tissue injury rather than immune amnesia.
Malnutrition impairs immunity, with function potentially restored by adequate nutrition. It would fit a reversible nutritional cause without memory-cell destruction.
Immunosuppressive treatment creates secondary immunodeficiency by medically suppressing immune activity. It would fit therapy for transplantation, autoimmunity, or cancer.
Measles causes immune amnesia by destroying memory B and T cells, with substantial antibody loss and increased susceptibility lasting several years.

question: Which finding favors a primary immunodeficiency over an acquired immunocompromised state?
cited_learning_objective: Compare & contrast the etiology and typical presentation for major primary and secondary immunodeficiencies

options.rationale: Post-transplant infections are associated with immunosuppressive therapy, an acquired cause. This would support secondary immunodeficiency.
Large burns produce acquired immune compromise through barrier loss and cytokine release. This would support a secondary cause.
Early-onset recurrent infections with a family pattern support an inherited mutation causing primary immunodeficiency.
Dialysis is a biochemical-homeostasis disorder associated with secondary immunodeficiency. This would favor an acquired rather than inherited state.
Ionizing radiation is an environmental cause of secondary immunodeficiency. This would favor external immune injury.

question: A 4-month-old boy has chronic diarrhea, poor growth, and recurrent bacterial, fungal, and viral infections. Flow cytometry shows absent T cells with preserved B cell numbers, and serum antibodies are low. Which defect is most likely?
cited_learning_objective: Utilizing the patient presentation and common diagnostic test results, determine and differentiate between the various primary immunodeficiencies given a clinical case

options.rationale: The early combined infection pattern, absent T cells, preserved B cells, and low antibodies match X-linked SCID caused by a common gamma-chain signaling defect.
RAG deficiency prevents antigen-receptor rearrangement and removes both T and B cells. It would fit absent T cells and absent B cells.

Adenosine deaminase deficiency causes toxic metabolite accumulation with reduced T cells and reduced B cells. It would fit combined lymphocyte loss, potentially with early neurologic or hearing abnormalities.
MHC II deficiency predominantly reduces CD4 cells while preserving CD8 and B cells. It would fit selective CD4 reduction rather than complete T cell absence.
BTK deficiency removes mature B cells while preserving T cells and usually presents after six months. It would fit absent B cells with bacterial infections.

question: A 6-month-old infant has recurrent opportunistic infections, chronic diarrhea, and failure to thrive. Flow cytometry shows no T cells, and chest imaging shows no thymic shadow. Which definitive intervention is most appropriate?
cited_learning_objective: Identify immunodeficiency treatments for categories of immunodeficiencies

options.rationale: Immunoglobulin can supply antibodies but does not restore the absent T cell compartment. It would be primary therapy for an isolated antibody deficiency such as BTK-related agammaglobulinemia.
The findings indicate SCID, for which hematopoietic stem cell transplantation can restore immune-cell development after immediate infections are controlled.
Routine vaccination does not reconstruct the profoundly deficient cellular immune system. Vaccination is emphasized for complement deficiencies and prevention in selected secondary states.
Prophylaxis may reduce infection risk but is insufficient as definitive treatment for untreated SCID. It would be appropriate as part of infection control in some phagocyte disorders.

options.text: Prompt antibiotics during symptomatic infections only
options.rationale: Reactive antimicrobial treatment does not correct the lethal combined immune defect. It would be an adjunct for a presenting infection, not definitive management.

question: A newborn has hypocalcemic tetany, a cleft palate, abnormal facial features, and recurrent infections. Flow cytometry shows reduced T cells with preserved B cells. Which intervention addresses the principal developmental immune defect?
cited_learning_objective: Identify immunodeficiency treatments for categories of immunodeficiencies

options.rationale: Immunoglobulin provides passive antibodies but does not replace the underdeveloped thymic environment. It would fit a primary antibody-production disorder.
Prophylaxis may help selected patients but does not address absent thymic development. It would be central to aggressive infection control in chronic granulomatous disease.
The CATCH-22 pattern indicates DiGeorge syndrome with thymic aplasia, for which thymic transplantation is the preferred intervention in complete disease.
Lung transplantation may be used for severe lung destruction in MHC I deficiency. It does not correct thymic aplasia.
Vaccination and prompt antibiotics are emphasized for complement deficiencies but do not reconstruct an absent thymus. They would fit a complement-mediated infection risk.

question: A 7-year-old child has recurrent viral respiratory infections, vasculitic skin lesions, normal antibody levels, low CD8 cells, and normal CD4 cells. Which molecular abnormality is most likely?
cited_learning_objective: Utilizing the patient presentation and common diagnostic test results, determine and differentiate between the various primary immunodeficiencies given a clinical case

options.rationale: MHC II deficiency reduces CD4 cells and IgG while preserving CD8 cells. It would fit severe combined infections beginning shortly after birth.
Common gamma-chain deficiency causes SCID with absent T cells and low antibodies. It would fit profound disease in early infancy.
CD40L deficiency preserves lymphocyte counts but prevents class switching. It would fit increased IgM with deficiency of other isotypes.
A TAP mutation causes MHC I deficiency, producing low CD8 cells, preserved CD4 cells and antibodies, recurrent respiratory infections, and skin lesions.
BTK deficiency causes absent mature B cells and low levels of all antibodies. It would fit bacterial infections beginning at 6-18 months.

question: A 3-year-old boy has recurrent pneumonia and sinusitis caused by encapsulated bacteria. Flow cytometry shows markedly reduced B cells, normal T cells, and serum testing shows low levels of every antibody class. Which treatment is most appropriate?
cited_learning_objective: Identify immunodeficiency treatments for categories of immunodeficiencies

options.rationale: The pattern identifies BTK-related agammaglobulinemia, and regular IVIG replaces antibodies that the absent mature B cell compartment cannot produce.
Thymic transplantation treats complete thymic aplasia rather than isolated B cell failure. It would fit DiGeorge syndrome with marked T cell deficiency.
Antifungal prophylaxis does not replace the broadly absent antibodies. It would be part of infection prevention in chronic granulomatous disease.
Vaccination and prompt antibiotics are used for complement defects but do not reliably replace missing immunoglobulins. This would fit terminal complement deficiency.
Stem cell transplantation is not the listed standard treatment for BTK-related agammaglobulinemia. It would be definitive therapy for SCID or severe phagocyte disorders.

question: A 2-year-old boy has recurrent pulmonary infections from encapsulated bacteria and opportunistic organisms. B and T cell counts are normal, but IgM is increased while other antibody isotypes are deficient. Which cellular interaction is impaired?
cited_learning_objective: Utilizing the patient presentation and common diagnostic test results, determine and differentiate between the various primary immunodeficiencies given a clinical case

options.rationale: Defective BCR signaling from a BTK mutation prevents mature B cell development. It would fit reduced B cells and low levels of all antibody classes.

options.text: MHC I presentation to CD8 cells
options.rationale: Defective MHC I presentation reduces CD8 cells while preserving antibody levels. It would fit recurrent viral respiratory disease and vasculitic skin lesions.

options.text: MHC II presentation to CD4 cells
options.rationale: Defective MHC II expression reduces CD4 cells and IgG. It would fit low CD4 counts with normal CD8 and B cell numbers.
CD40L on T cells supplies the CD40 signal required for B cell class switching and affinity maturation; its absence produces the hyper-IgM pattern.
TAP deficiency causes MHC I deficiency and reduced CD8 cells rather than failed antibody class switching. It would fit normal antibody isotypes with low CD8 cells.

question: A 6-year-old child has recurrent sinus and gastrointestinal infections. B and T cell counts are normal. IgA is low, while all other antibody isotypes are normal. Which additional precaution is most important?
cited_learning_objective: Identify immunodeficiency treatments for categories of immunodeficiencies

options.rationale: Selective IgA deficiency can produce anti-IgA antibodies, creating a risk of hypersensitivity reactions during blood transfusion.
Most patients with selective IgA deficiency are asymptomatic and require no treatment; routine IVIG is not the listed management. It would fit broad antibody deficiency.
Thymic transplantation addresses complete thymic aplasia and T cell deficiency. It would fit DiGeorge syndrome rather than isolated low IgA.
Lifelong antibacterial and antifungal prophylaxis is used for disorders such as chronic granulomatous disease. It is not routine for isolated IgA deficiency.

options.text: Arrange urgent hematopoietic stem cell transplantation
options.rationale: Stem cell transplantation is reserved for severe immune defects and is not listed for selective IgA deficiency. It would fit SCID or severe leukocyte adhesion deficiency.

question: A 3-year-old boy has recurrent bacterial and fungal infections with obstructing gastrointestinal granulomas. His neutrophil count is elevated. Dihydrorhodamine testing shows no fluorescence shift after stimulation. Which defect explains these findings?
cited_learning_objective: Utilizing the patient presentation and common diagnostic test results, determine and differentiate between the various primary immunodeficiencies given a clinical case

options.rationale: Adhesion-molecule deficiency prevents extravasation and causes absent pus and poor healing. It would fit delayed umbilical separation rather than an abnormal oxidative-burst assay.
LYST deficiency causes giant cytoplasmic granules, partial albinism, and neurologic disease. It would fit abnormal granule morphology on the blood smear.
Failure of NADPH oxidase prevents superoxide and reactive oxygen species production, causing defective phagocyte killing, recurrent bacterial and fungal infections, and granuloma formation.
Terminal complement deficiency predisposes specifically to recurrent Neisseria infections. It would fit a low CH50 rather than absent dihydrorhodamine conversion.
Deficient BCR signaling from BTK mutation reduces mature B cells and antibodies. It would fit recurrent encapsulated bacterial infections without fungal susceptibility or granulomas.

question: A child with recurrent bacterial and fungal infections is diagnosed after absent neutrophil conversion of a fluorescent respiratory-burst substrate. Which long-term management strategy is indicated?
cited_learning_objective: Identify immunodeficiency treatments for categories of immunodeficiencies

options.rationale: Antibody replacement does not correct defective phagocyte killing. It would fit a broad antibody deficiency with low immunoglobulin levels.
Vaccination and prompt treatment are emphasized for complement deficiencies but provide insufficient prevention for chronic granulomatous disease.
Thymic transplantation treats complete DiGeorge syndrome. It would fit thymic aplasia with hypocalcemia and reduced T cells.
Chronic granulomatous disease requires lifelong antibacterial and antifungal prophylaxis with early aggressive treatment of infections; stem cell transplantation may provide a definitive cure.
Transfusion precautions are important in selective IgA deficiency but do not address defective respiratory burst. They would fit isolated low IgA with possible anti-IgA antibodies.

question: A 2-year-old child has recurrent bacterial infections, light-colored hair, progressive neurologic abnormalities, and giant granules in leukocytes and platelets. Which treatment can correct the immune component but not the nonimmune findings?
cited_learning_objective: Identify immunodeficiency treatments for categories of immunodeficiencies

options.rationale: IVIG replaces deficient antibodies but does not repair lysosomal trafficking in leukocytes. It would fit agammaglobulinemia or hyper-IgM syndrome.
This strategy reduces infection risk in complement deficiencies but does not correct the underlying granule-trafficking defect.
The findings identify Chédiak-Higashi syndrome; hematopoietic stem cell transplantation corrects its immune component but not the nonimmune manifestations.
Thymic transplantation treats thymic aplasia rather than defective lysosomal trafficking. It would fit complete DiGeorge syndrome.
Lung transplantation may be considered after severe lung damage in MHC I deficiency. It does not correct systemic leukocyte granule dysfunction.

question: A newborn develops omphalitis, and the umbilical cord remains attached beyond 30 days. Later bacterial skin infections heal poorly and produce no pus despite elevated blood neutrophils. Which diagnostic test is most appropriate?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the principles of flow cytometry, and interpret flow cytometric dot plots to identify specific leukocyte populations (review common WBC markers learned in Block 1)

options.rationale: Delayed cord separation, absent pus, poor healing, and circulating neutrophilia indicate leukocyte adhesion deficiency, evaluated by flow cytometric detection of adhesion molecules such as LFA-1 CD18.
Respiratory-burst testing evaluates chronic granulomatous disease, in which neutrophils reach tissue but kill poorly. It would fit granulomas and bacterial or fungal infections.
IgA testing evaluates selective IgA deficiency and does not explain absent tissue neutrophils. It would fit recurrent mucosal infections after age four years.
A smear for giant granules evaluates Chédiak-Higashi syndrome. It would fit partial albinism and progressive neurologic findings.
CH50 evaluates classical complement activity. It would fit recurrent bacterial or Neisseria infections with normal leukocyte trafficking.

question: An infant with severe leukocyte adhesion deficiency has recurrent invasive infections despite aggressive prophylaxis. Which next intervention offers the best prognosis before severe infections accumulate?
cited_learning_objective: Identify immunodeficiency treatments for categories of immunodeficiencies

options.rationale: IVIG replaces antibodies but does not restore leukocyte adhesion and extravasation. It would fit a primary antibody deficiency.
Severe leukocyte adhesion deficiency requires hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, with better prognosis when performed before severe infections occur.
Thymic transplantation corrects complete thymic aplasia rather than adhesion-molecule deficiency. It would fit DiGeorge syndrome.
Vaccination and prompt antibiotics are central for complement deficiency but are insufficient for severe leukocyte adhesion deficiency.
Lung transplantation may address severe pulmonary damage in MHC I deficiency but does not restore leukocyte extravasation.

question: A 5-year-old child has recurrent sinopulmonary infections, bacteremia, and meningitis caused by gram-negative bacteria. Symptoms began shortly after birth. Which laboratory abnormality is most likely?
cited_learning_objective: Utilizing the patient presentation and common diagnostic test results, determine and differentiate between the various primary immunodeficiencies given a clinical case

options.rationale: C3 deficiency presents shortly after birth with recurrent bacterial sinopulmonary disease, bacteremia, or meningitis, especially involving gram-negative organisms.
Low CD8 cells characterize MHC I deficiency, which more often causes recurrent viral respiratory infections and skin lesions. It would fit normal antibody levels and preserved CD4 cells.
Low B cells suggest BTK-related agammaglobulinemia, which usually becomes apparent at 6-18 months. It would fit low levels of all antibody classes.
Absent dihydrorhodamine conversion indicates chronic granulomatous disease. It would fit bacterial and fungal infections with granuloma formation.
Absent CD18 supports leukocyte adhesion deficiency. It would fit delayed umbilical separation, absent pus, and poor wound healing.

question: A 14-year-old has a second meningococcal infection. White blood cell counts and antibody levels are normal. Which initial test is most appropriate?
cited_learning_objective: Utilizing the patient presentation and common diagnostic test results, determine and differentiate between the various primary immunodeficiencies given a clinical case

options.rationale: Antibody levels are already normal, and recurrent Neisseria infections point toward complement dysfunction. This test would be appropriate for suspected humoral deficiency.
Lymphocyte enumeration evaluates B and T cell deficiencies but does not assess late complement function. It would fit broad viral, fungal, or opportunistic susceptibility.
Dihydrorhodamine testing evaluates respiratory burst in chronic granulomatous disease. It would fit recurrent catalase-positive bacterial and fungal infections.
Recurrent Neisseria infection with normal leukocytes and antibodies warrants CH50 screening of classical complement pathway activity before individual components are measured.
Adhesion-molecule genotyping evaluates leukocyte adhesion deficiency. It would fit neonatal-onset infections with delayed cord separation and absent pus.

question: An 8-year-old with recurrent bacterial respiratory infections also develops manifestations of systemic lupus erythematosus. Which group of deficient proteins best explains both findings?
cited_learning_objective: Utilizing the patient presentation and common diagnostic test results, determine and differentiate between the various primary immunodeficiencies given a clinical case

options.rationale: C6 through C9 deficiencies predominantly cause recurrent Neisseria infections. They would fit meningococcal or gonococcal recurrence without the characteristic lupus association.
Deficiencies of early classical pathway components C1, C2, or C4 are associated with childhood bacterial infections and systemic lupus erythematosus.
CD18 deficiency impairs leukocyte extravasation and causes absent pus and poor wound healing. It would fit delayed umbilical separation.
RAG deficiency prevents receptor rearrangement and causes SCID with absent B and T cells. It would fit severe infections beginning in infancy.
Common gamma-chain deficiency causes X-linked SCID with absent T cells and low antibodies. It would fit profound opportunistic disease in a male infant.

question: A patient receiving immunosuppressive therapy after organ transplantation develops recurrent infections. Genetic testing for inherited immune defects is unrevealing. Which classification best describes this condition?
cited_learning_objective: List secondary causes of immunocompromised states

options.rationale: Primary combined immunodeficiency arises from inherited mutations affecting T and B cell function. It would fit early severe infections with an identifiable genetic defect.
Primary cellular immunodeficiency results from inherited defects affecting T cell development or function. It would fit a congenital cellular abnormality rather than treatment exposure.
Immunosuppressive therapy after transplantation is an external medical factor and therefore causes a secondary acquired immunodeficiency.
Primary antibody deficiency results from inherited B cell or antibody abnormalities. It would fit low immunoglobulins or absent B cells arising independently of treatment.
Primary phagocyte disorders result from mutations affecting killing, trafficking, or extravasation. They would fit a characteristic congenital phagocyte phenotype.

question: A severely malnourished patient develops frequent infections without an identified immune-system mutation. Nutritional rehabilitation is initiated. Which outcome is most consistent with the underlying mechanism?
cited_learning_objective: List secondary causes of immunocompromised states

options.text: Persistent absence of mature B cells
options.rationale: Persistent absence of mature B cells suggests an inherited BTK defect. It would fit primary agammaglobulinemia rather than reversible malnutrition.
Thymic aplasia is a congenital developmental abnormality in DiGeorge syndrome. It would fit reduced T cells with CATCH-22 features.
Malnutrition is a secondary cause of immune compromise, and improved nutrition can restore immune function because the defect is externally acquired.
Persistent class-switch failure suggests a CD40L, CD40, or AID defect. It would fit increased IgM with deficiency of other isotypes.
Absent respiratory burst indicates inherited NADPH oxidase dysfunction and would not normalize through nutrition. It would fit chronic granulomatous disease.

question: A child recovering from measles later develops infections from pathogens previously controlled by immune memory. Testing demonstrates a major reduction in preexisting antibodies. Which mechanism best explains the prolonged susceptibility?
cited_learning_objective: List secondary causes of immunocompromised states

options.text: Exhaustion of humoral and cellular responses
options.rationale: Immune exhaustion affecting humoral and cellular responses is associated with chronic malaria. It would fit persistent malaria rather than post-measles loss of prior immunity.

options.text: Loss of memory B and T cells
options.rationale: Measles can destroy memory B and T cells, causing immune amnesia, substantial loss of existing antibodies, and susceptibility lasting several years.

options.text: Failure of leukocyte adhesion and trafficking
options.rationale: Adhesion failure is an inherited leukocyte trafficking disorder. It would fit absent pus, poor healing, and delayed umbilical separation.
Toxic metabolite accumulation occurs in adenosine deaminase deficiency. It would fit early SCID with reduced T and B cells.
Class-switch failure produces elevated IgM and deficiency of other isotypes. It would fit hyper-IgM syndrome rather than loss of previously established antibodies.

question: A child has recurrent bacterial infections, normal leukocyte counts, and normal antibody levels. CH50 is low. Individual testing shows deficiency of a late pathway component. Which prevention strategy is most appropriate?
cited_learning_objective: Identify immunodeficiency treatments for categories of immunodeficiencies

options.rationale: Immunoglobulin replacement treats deficient antibody production, while this patient has normal antibody levels. It would fit agammaglobulinemia or hyper-IgM syndrome.
Thymic transplantation treats complete thymic aplasia rather than complement deficiency. It would fit DiGeorge syndrome with severe T cell deficiency.
Late complement deficiencies are managed with vaccination plus prompt identification and antibiotic treatment of infections, particularly those caused by Neisseria.
Antifungal prophylaxis and respiratory-burst testing apply to chronic granulomatous disease. They would fit recurrent bacterial and fungal infections with defective NADPH oxidase.
Stem cell transplantation is not the listed routine treatment for late complement deficiency. It would fit SCID or severe leukocyte adhesion deficiency.
